ILLEGAL LAND SALES

By: Ntokozo Miya | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Many of Gauteng's 700 informal settlements were set up illegally – we investigate how syndicates distribute and sell land owned by municipalities or private individuals.

Unique Selling Point:
Covering around 3500 hectares of land, the Crocodile River Reserve used to be home to a range of wildlife including scorpions, birds, frogs, bats and gazelle. About 100 local landowners initiated a process to have the reserve declared a protected area and last year, they succeeded. In October, the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development announced that the reserve in Centurion, outside Pretoria, would be protected from human activity that could cause harm to the flora and fauna as well as the environment.

Less than a year later, the area has suffered exactly that – harm caused by human activity, criminal human activity to be exact.

Seeing a lucrative market out of people's desperation for land and housing, a man by the name of Baba Sashane, who does not own any land on the reserve, started a land sales business on the conservation area. Sashane sells 20m by 20m plots on protected land that does not belong to him, and business is booming at R10 000 per plot.

A large area within the reserve is now a fully-fledged informal settlement with a creche, supermarkets and even a taxi route. Rightful landowners are helpless to remove the squatters.

The forest is quickly being stripped of its trees for firewood – there is no formal electricity supply to the settlement so the fast-growing community relies on wood fires to cook and keep warm in the brutal winter. Wildlife including species of buck have been hunted to near non-existence by the newcomers.

A local business has reported several robberies in recent months and has had to shut down their evening service offerings due to safety concerns.

Summary:

Seeing a lucrative market out of people's desperation for land and housing, a man by the name of Baba Sashane, who does not own any land on the reserve, started a land sales business on the conservation area. Sashane sells 20m by 20m plots on protected land that does not belong to him, and business is booming at R10 000 per plot.

A large area within the reserve is now a fully-fledged informal settlement with a creche, supermarkets and even a taxi route. Rightful landowners are helpless to remove the squatters.

The forest is quickly being stripped of its trees for firewood – there is no formal electricity supply to the settlement so the fast-growing community relies on wood fires to cook and keep warm in the brutal winter. Wildlife including species of buck have been hunted to near non-existence by the newcomers.

A local business has reported several robberies in recent months and has had to shut down their evening service offerings due to safety concerns.

Further information:
We also revisit Lenasia to see if authorities managed to clamp down on the illegal sale of municipal land following our previous broadcast on the matter. They did not.

In fact, since our last report, syndicates have become more brazen. And in the lockdown, while all law enforcement eyes were on managing densely populated spaces, vacant land outside of Lenasia was once again up for illegal sales.

Our research showed that the Phumla Mqashi informal settlement near Lenasia is one of the most problematic as the city of Joburg has repeatedly evicted people from the area but every time the dust settles after evictions, people always return to rebuild – we set about finding out why they keep coming back?

It turns out a syndicate advertises on Facebook: “...if you need a stand there's a place where a owner is selling stand with 250. He used to have a farm now his giving it to people by 250 only cause his tired of people who kill people and damp them there so please contact me at 0815671581 I will take you there...”

We responded to this advert and captured the interaction and sales pitch on hidden camera.

To illustrate the prevalence of the illegal sale of land in Gauteng, we highlight the recent events in Elandsfonten in the Vaal. The Vaal community is especially interesting because the rightful property owners banded together to force the municipality into action against the land invaders.

Also, they documented the events and their efforts exceptionally well, even getting their own hidden camera footage to expose the land sellers who were eventually arrested. Here, land was sold at R1 000 per plot and the sales pitch was filmed by a community member.

They also have footage of the evictions enforced by the municipal police, army and the Red Ants. It's a great story of the lengths to which a community went in order to prevent an informal settlement from mushrooming, literally, on their stoep.

Though, the syndicate keeps trying to make a return to the area, it's in dribs and drabs and such evictions easier to manage than having to evict a small township.

Extra Budget Items:
We have gotten a quote of R4 877.50 from Bad Boyz Security to have two armed guards accompany us on the day we will be doing confrontations. We have since requested a discount and will advise ASAP if they apply it. We have given the brief that guards are not to interfere with proceedings but only to watch from a reasonable distance. It has been made clear that they are there more for visibility and to keep an eye on us and NOT be a part of the interactions.

Script:


ILLEGAL LAND SALES


VO – Ten years ago, Jonathan Anderson moved his family away from the bustling city, to the quiet farming community of Elandsfontein, south-east of Johannesburg.

JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER
We've got ducks, geese and chickens. We get up in the mornings and we feed the horses and take the horses out into the field.

VO – Part of Anderson's plot is the family's living quarters, while the bigger open space is reserved for grazing.

On the 4th of June, the family's peaceful existence was interrupted.

JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER
We just saw smoke coming through our front door. We rushed out and saw that the whole field was on fire. There was a whole bunch of people. They were setting the fires.

VO - On the neighbouring plot, a makeshift office had been set up overnight. Its occupants were selling off plots to buyers who were setting fires to clear the land to build shacks. In disbelief, the original landowners secretly recorded the sales pitch.

UPSOUND
BUYER – What do I need to bring to get a plot?
SELLER - We need your ID, a copy of your ID and R1 000.

VO - This land is privately owned, and not for sale. Some buyers knew that the land was being sold illegally while others had no idea.

LINK – As of 2019, there were 700 informal settlements in Gauteng, but the number is rising quickly and private landowners say the illegal sale of land has a lot to do with that spike.

VO – Government's inability to provide adequate housing has created a lucrative market for criminal syndicates that prey on people who are desperate for homes.

In August last year, we investigated the mushrooming of informal settlements around Lenasia in Johannesburg South, where money was also exchanging hands.

UPSOUND – CB ARCHIVE – AUGUST 2019
SELLER - Ok, the ground is for free. You contribute R1 500 for development in the place.

VO – This year, the problem seems to have spread.
Now, buyers are enticed by adverts like this one, showing a farmer selling plots for two hundred and fifty rands.
So we responded to the ad and were directed to Tsietsi at Lenasia's Phumla Mqashi settlement.

TSIETSI – SELLER
BUYER – It was advertised for R250.
SELLER – That's just to show gratitude. That's for the lawyers at the office. It's not R250. That's just to say 'thank you' but stands go for at least R1 000.

VO – But plots in Phumla Mqashi were sold out, so we were shown stands across the highway in Elandsfontein. Though the land is vacant, it belongs to private owners, among them, Jonathan Anderson.

LINK - With all law enforcement eyes set on densely populated areas during the lockdown, vacant spaces have once again been targeted by greedy syndicates.

VO – Elandsfontein landowner Werner Maree says settlers dug pit toilets on his homestead and ignored requests to vacate his property.

WERNER MAREE – PROPERTY OWNER
I showed them my title deed, what I have got for my property. It's just that they don't give a flying hell about it.

VO – Community leader Clinton Gruar is on the frontlines of the fight against the developing informal settlement.

CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER
I eventually then got half the community together and we went to the De Deur police station as a group to force them to open a case.

VO – Residents managed to get a court order to have the shacks demolished before anyone moved in. Three weeks ago, the structures were destroyed and eleven people were arrested for trespassing.
Landowners hoped this would be the end of their ordeal...
But while the issue is long-standing in Joburg south, it's popping up all over Gauteng, close to economic opportunities.

LINK – Even protected conservation areas are under threat as syndicates brazenly go about their illegal land trade, with no care for the law.

The Crocodile River Reserve on the edge of Gauteng's boundary with the North West province is home to more than three hundred bird species, among other fauna and flora. It was declared a protected area last year. Jennifer Cornish serves on the reserve's management team.

JENNIFER CORNISH – CROCODILE RIVER RESERVE
What we're looking at now is called Egoli granite grassland - that is also listed threatened species. There's probably about six percent of it left.

VO – The reserve borders on one of Pretoria’s oldest townships, Atteridgeville. Illicit land sales and shack-building on its outskirts has spilled right onto the reserve.

JENNIFER CORNISH – CROCODILE RIVER RESERVE
The amount of plundering of indigenous trees has been very extensive.

VO – Without electricity, many of the reserve's newest residents rely on wood fires to cook and keep warm.
Having more people on the reserve has resulted in wildlife poaching and river pollution. But this is still prime land and plots are expensive. Our enquiries led us to Baba Sashane.

UPSOUND – BABA SASHANE
SELLER - The plots are 20m by 20m.
HIDDEN CAM BUYER – 20m by 20m for how much?
SELLER – R10 000.

VO – Even though he does not own this land, Sashane denied any wrongdoing. He first agreed to an interview ...but seemed to change his mind.

LINK – [voicemail message]... Well, we were trying to get a hold of Bab' Sashane but it seems his phone is off. He was supposed to have met with us and now, we can't get a hold of him.

VO – This self-employed mother of two used her life savings to invest in private property in the reserve in the 1990s.

PROPERTY OWNER
When you're living such a busy lifestyle to come back to this and just be with nature, it's just beautiful.

VO – The syndicate illegally connects some buyers to the reserve's electricity supply lines, hiking the bills of rightful property owners and causing frequent power outages.
When municipal workers recently inspected the prohibited connections in the reserve, settlers desperate to have electricity allegedly stoned their cars and injured them in the process of chasing them away.

PROPERTY OWNER
I blame government because they haven't done what they should have done. They need to take care of the people.

VO – She worries that the encroaching informal settlement will destroy the value of her investment.

LINK - Despite the suspension of evictions during the lockdown, the human settlements department says it has a plan to eradicate land invasions.

VO – Gauteng Human Settlements MEC, Lebogang Maile says the lockdown moratorium only applies to evictions and demolitions of occupied structures.

LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC
There's new people who have been trying to occupy recently and we have been working on stopping those people from occupying these pieces of land.

VO – Taking advantage of the moratorium on evictions of occupied structures, sellers urge buyers to erect and occupy shacks as quickly as possible.

LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC

MAC - In just 3 days, as a team we were able to meet with at least 11 different sellers. The guys are brazenly selling illegal land and you can't get a grip on it?
MEC - The city of Joburg and Tshwane did away with their land invasion units and it's only now that the land invasion units are being revived by these two cities because without a dedicated unit that deals with this, we'll not be able to crack this and deal with these criminals decisively.

VO – More than three hundred thousand people flock to Gauteng each year, many in need of homes. Not everybody will get a house but through the Rapid Land Release Program, some might get land.

LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC
Those who can build for themselves can have access to land. We are able to give them stands which have water, electricity and other services but to suggest that we will solve this overnight, I'd be lying to citizens.

VO - For the community of Elandsfontein, the story was far from over. The determined shack-dwellers returned and a tense standoff ensued.

UPSOUND
Land sellers and buyers marching, singing, with garden tools and such

VO – Lethu Masoka is the spokesperson for land-sellers and buyers in Joburg South, including the team we met in Phumla Mqashi. In a shocking twist, Masoka named the farmer he said is referred to in their Facebook advert.

LETHU MASOKA – SELLER
Clinton took us in his car, an X5, and . He drove us around this place and showed us where we can build our shacks. He even supplied us with spotlights for our patrol car. Bring him here and ask him what he said to me.

VO – And so we did - ironically, Clinton Gruar now feared for his safety and called for some backup to stand between him and Masoka.

CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER
Yes, I did take them around and show them the properties. I explained to them that these properties are privately owned properties. We cannot just build as we please.

VO – Though Gruar is leading the charge against the land grab, he admits that he did give a helping hand to the so-called invaders.

CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER
They asked me to buy them a spotlight so that they can do patrols which I have not done yet. I did give them my patrol lights which was on my vehicle for the so-called patrolling that they were supposed to have done, which he never did.

VO – Gruar denies that he conspired with Masoka and his group against his own community.
Masoka later explained why they charge R250 for land they do not own.

LETHU MASOKA – SELLER
This covers petrol costs, paying people to allocate plots and guard shacks.
MAC - If a private owner comes to you and says I understand you want to come stay here but I don't want you on my land, will you then say: “Okay, we'll move somewhere else.”
LETHU – We do not work that way, my brother. Here, we don’t work like that.

VO – Masoka insists that his group chose land in this area simply because it is vacant.

LETHU MASOKA – SELLER
MAC - I can't come to your house and say that you have space in your backyard so I will put up my shack here.
LETHU – The reason we are bringing people here is that they are not using the land.

VO – Landowners whose properties are invaded are advised to “approach the court without delay for an eviction order”.
Both sides of the Elandsfontein standoff believe they will prevail and be the last landowner standing.

JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER
If nobody is selling our lands, then nobody will buy the land and they won't be here.

PROMOS

The land is cheap, the transactions are quick and shacks go up within hours – we expose
the workings of criminal syndicates that sell land that does not belong to them.



Syndicates selling land they do not own go up against landowners resisting
informal settlements on their properties – a standoff fuelled by housing shortages across
Gauteng.

Housing backlogs have created fertile ground for desperate people to be duped into
buying plots of land from criminal syndicates who don't own the sites they're selling.

Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 16 September 2020 Script: ILLEGAL LAND SALES VO – Ten years ago, Jonathan Anderson moved his family away from the bustling city, to the quiet farming community of Elandsfontein, south-east of Johannesburg. JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER We've got ducks, geese and chickens. We get up in the mornings and we feed the horses and take the horses out into the field. VO – Part of Anderson's plot is the family's living quarters, while the bigger open space is reserved for grazing. On the 4th of June, the family's peaceful existence was interrupted. JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER We just saw smoke coming through our front door. We rushed out and saw that the whole field was on fire. There was a whole bunch of people. They were setting the fires. VO - On the neighbouring plot, a makeshift office had been set up overnight. Its occupants were selling off plots to buyers who were setting fires to clear the land to build shacks. In disbelief, the original landowners secretly recorded the sales pitch. UPSOUND BUYER – What do I need to bring to get a plot? SELLER - We need your ID, a copy of your ID and R1 000. VO - This land is privately owned, and not for sale. Some buyers knew that the land was being sold illegally while others had no idea. LINK – As of 2019, there were 700 informal settlements in Gauteng, but the number is rising quickly and private landowners say the illegal sale of land has a lot to do with that spike. VO – Government's inability to provide adequate housing has created a lucrative market for criminal syndicates that prey on people who are desperate for homes. In August last year, we investigated the mushrooming of informal settlements around Lenasia in Johannesburg South, where money was also exchanging hands. UPSOUND – CB ARCHIVE – AUGUST 2019 SELLER - Ok, the ground is for free. You contribute R1 500 for development in the place. VO – This year, the problem seems to have spread. Now, buyers are enticed by adverts like this one, showing a farmer selling plots for two hundred and fifty rands. So we responded to the ad and were directed to Tsietsi at Lenasia's Phumla Mqashi settlement. TSIETSI – SELLER BUYER – It was advertised for R250. SELLER – That's just to show gratitude. That's for the lawyers at the office. It's not R250. That's just to say 'thank you' but stands go for at least R1 000. VO – But plots in Phumla Mqashi were sold out, so we were shown stands across the highway in Elandsfontein. Though the land is vacant, it belongs to private owners, among them, Jonathan Anderson. LINK - With all law enforcement eyes set on densely populated areas during the lockdown, vacant spaces have once again been targeted by greedy syndicates. VO – Elandsfontein landowner Werner Maree says settlers dug pit toilets on his homestead and ignored requests to vacate his property. WERNER MAREE – PROPERTY OWNER I showed them my title deed, what I have got for my property. It's just that they don't give a flying hell about it. VO – Community leader Clinton Gruar is on the frontlines of the fight against the developing informal settlement. CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER I eventually then got half the community together and we went to the De Deur police station as a group to force them to open a case. VO – Residents managed to get a court order to have the shacks demolished before anyone moved in. Three weeks ago, the structures were destroyed and eleven people were arrested for trespassing. Landowners hoped this would be the end of their ordeal... But while the issue is long-standing in Joburg south, it's popping up all over Gauteng, close to economic opportunities. LINK – Even protected conservation areas are under threat as syndicates brazenly go about their illegal land trade, with no care for the law. The Crocodile River Reserve on the edge of Gauteng's boundary with the North West province is home to more than three hundred bird species, among other fauna and flora. It was declared a protected area last year. Jennifer Cornish serves on the reserve's management team. JENNIFER CORNISH – CROCODILE RIVER RESERVE What we're looking at now is called Egoli granite grassland - that is also listed threatened species. There's probably about six percent of it left. VO – The reserve borders on one of Pretoria’s oldest townships, Atteridgeville. Illicit land sales and shack-building on its outskirts has spilled right onto the reserve. JENNIFER CORNISH – CROCODILE RIVER RESERVE The amount of plundering of indigenous trees has been very extensive. VO – Without electricity, many of the reserve's newest residents rely on wood fires to cook and keep warm. Having more people on the reserve has resulted in wildlife poaching and river pollution. But this is still prime land and plots are expensive. Our enquiries led us to Baba Sashane. UPSOUND – BABA SASHANE SELLER - The plots are 20m by 20m. HIDDEN CAM BUYER – 20m by 20m for how much? SELLER – R10 000. VO – Even though he does not own this land, Sashane denied any wrongdoing. He first agreed to an interview ...but seemed to change his mind. LINK – [voicemail message]... Well, we were trying to get a hold of Bab' Sashane but it seems his phone is off. He was supposed to have met with us and now, we can't get a hold of him. VO – This self-employed mother of two used her life savings to invest in private property in the reserve in the 1990s. PROPERTY OWNER When you're living such a busy lifestyle to come back to this and just be with nature, it's just beautiful. VO – The syndicate illegally connects some buyers to the reserve's electricity supply lines, hiking the bills of rightful property owners and causing frequent power outages. When municipal workers recently inspected the prohibited connections in the reserve, settlers desperate to have electricity allegedly stoned their cars and injured them in the process of chasing them away. PROPERTY OWNER I blame government because they haven't done what they should have done. They need to take care of the people. VO – She worries that the encroaching informal settlement will destroy the value of her investment. LINK - Despite the suspension of evictions during the lockdown, the human settlements department says it has a plan to eradicate land invasions. VO – Gauteng Human Settlements MEC, Lebogang Maile says the lockdown moratorium only applies to evictions and demolitions of occupied structures. LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC There's new people who have been trying to occupy recently and we have been working on stopping those people from occupying these pieces of land. VO – Taking advantage of the moratorium on evictions of occupied structures, sellers urge buyers to erect and occupy shacks as quickly as possible. LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC MAC - In just 3 days, as a team we were able to meet with at least 11 different sellers. The guys are brazenly selling illegal land and you can't get a grip on it? MEC - The city of Joburg and Tshwane did away with their land invasion units and it's only now that the land invasion units are being revived by these two cities because without a dedicated unit that deals with this, we'll not be able to crack this and deal with these criminals decisively. VO – More than three hundred thousand people flock to Gauteng each year, many in need of homes. Not everybody will get a house but through the Rapid Land Release Program, some might get land. LEBOGANG MAILE – GP HUMAN SETTLEMENTS MEC Those who can build for themselves can have access to land. We are able to give them stands which have water, electricity and other services but to suggest that we will solve this overnight, I'd be lying to citizens. VO - For the community of Elandsfontein, the story was far from over. The determined shack-dwellers returned and a tense standoff ensued. UPSOUND Land sellers and buyers marching, singing, with garden tools and such VO – Lethu Masoka is the spokesperson for land-sellers and buyers in Joburg South, including the team we met in Phumla Mqashi. In a shocking twist, Masoka named the farmer he said is referred to in their Facebook advert. LETHU MASOKA – SELLER Clinton took us in his car, an X5, and . He drove us around this place and showed us where we can build our shacks. He even supplied us with spotlights for our patrol car. Bring him here and ask him what he said to me. VO – And so we did - ironically, Clinton Gruar now feared for his safety and called for some backup to stand between him and Masoka. CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER Yes, I did take them around and show them the properties. I explained to them that these properties are privately owned properties. We cannot just build as we please. VO – Though Gruar is leading the charge against the land grab, he admits that he did give a helping hand to the so-called invaders. CLINTON GRUAR – ELANDSFONTEIN COMMUNITY LEADER They asked me to buy them a spotlight so that they can do patrols which I have not done yet. I did give them my patrol lights which was on my vehicle for the so-called patrolling that they were supposed to have done, which he never did. VO – Gruar denies that he conspired with Masoka and his group against his own community. Masoka later explained why they charge R250 for land they do not own. LETHU MASOKA – SELLER This covers petrol costs, paying people to allocate plots and guard shacks. MAC - If a private owner comes to you and says I understand you want to come stay here but I don't want you on my land, will you then say: “Okay, we'll move somewhere else.” LETHU – We do not work that way, my brother. Here, we don’t work like that. VO – Masoka insists that his group chose land in this area simply because it is vacant. LETHU MASOKA – SELLER MAC - I can't come to your house and say that you have space in your backyard so I will put up my shack here. LETHU – The reason we are bringing people here is that they are not using the land. VO – Landowners whose properties are invaded are advised to “approach the court without delay for an eviction order”. Both sides of the Elandsfontein standoff believe they will prevail and be the last landowner standing. JONATHAN ANDERSON – PROPERTY OWNER If nobody is selling our lands, then nobody will buy the land and they won't be here. PROMOS The land is cheap, the transactions are quick and shacks go up within hours – we expose the workings of criminal syndicates that sell land that does not belong to them. Syndicates selling land they do not own go up against landowners resisting informal settlements on their properties – a standoff fuelled by housing shortages across Gauteng. Housing backlogs have created fertile ground for desperate people to be duped into buying plots of land from criminal syndicates who don't own the sites they're selling.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Many of Gauteng's 700 informal settlements were set up illegally – we investigate how syndicates distribute and sell land owned by municipalities or private individuals.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Covering around 3500 hectares of land, the Crocodile River Reserve used to be home to a range of wildlife including scorpions, birds, frogs, bats and gazelle. About 100 local landowners initiated a process to have the reserve declared a protected area and last year, they succeeded. In October, the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development announced that the reserve in Centurion, outside Pretoria, would be protected from human activity that could cause harm to the flora and fauna as well as the environment. Less than a year later, the area has suffered exactly that – harm caused by human activity, criminal human activity to be exact. Seeing a lucrative market out of people's desperation for land and housing, a man by the name of Baba Sashane, who does not own any land on the reserve, started a land sales business on the conservation area. Sashane sells 20m by 20m plots on protected land that does not belong to him, and business is booming at R10 000 per plot. A large area within the reserve is now a fully-fledged informal settlement with a creche, supermarkets and even a taxi route. Rightful landowners are helpless to remove the squatters. The forest is quickly being stripped of its trees for firewood – there is no formal electricity supply to the settlement so the fast-growing community relies on wood fires to cook and keep warm in the brutal winter. Wildlife including species of buck have been hunted to near non-existence by the newcomers. A local business has reported several robberies in recent months and has had to shut down their evening service offerings due to safety concerns.

metadata.Further information: We also revisit Lenasia to see if authorities managed to clamp down on the illegal sale of municipal land following our previous broadcast on the matter. They did not. In fact, since our last report, syndicates have become more brazen. And in the lockdown, while all law enforcement eyes were on managing densely populated spaces, vacant land outside of Lenasia was once again up for illegal sales. Our research showed that the Phumla Mqashi informal settlement near Lenasia is one of the most problematic as the city of Joburg has repeatedly evicted people from the area but every time the dust settles after evictions, people always return to rebuild – we set about finding out why they keep coming back? It turns out a syndicate advertises on Facebook: “...if you need a stand there's a place where a owner is selling stand with 250. He used to have a farm now his giving it to people by 250 only cause his tired of people who kill people and damp them there so please contact me at 0815671581 I will take you there...” We responded to this advert and captured the interaction and sales pitch on hidden camera. To illustrate the prevalence of the illegal sale of land in Gauteng, we highlight the recent events in Elandsfonten in the Vaal. The Vaal community is especially interesting because the rightful property owners banded together to force the municipality into action against the land invaders. Also, they documented the events and their efforts exceptionally well, even getting their own hidden camera footage to expose the land sellers who were eventually arrested. Here, land was sold at R1 000 per plot and the sales pitch was filmed by a community member. They also have footage of the evictions enforced by the municipal police, army and the Red Ants. It's a great story of the lengths to which a community went in order to prevent an informal settlement from mushrooming, literally, on their stoep. Though, the syndicate keeps trying to make a return to the area, it's in dribs and drabs and such evictions easier to manage than having to evict a small township.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: We have gotten a quote of R4 877.50 from Bad Boyz Security to have two armed guards accompany us on the day we will be doing confrontations. We have since requested a discount and will advise ASAP if they apply it. We have given the brief that guards are not to interfere with proceedings but only to watch from a reasonable distance. It has been made clear that they are there more for visibility and to keep an eye on us and NOT be a part of the interactions.
